description: We are the team linked to Elisa aerospace and other. A groupe of engineering students interested in space exploration.
summary:
Elisapp is our new navigation software for Mars, designed for future explorers of the Red Planet and adapted for rover use. It operates locally relying exclusively on a satellite-based positioning system.
The algorithm is able to plan the user's EVA by taking into account all meteorological and topographical data as well as scientific missions and points of interest along the way. It keeps considering resource constraints, and adapts to offer the safest trip.
As safety is our top priority, we have designed a head-up display (HUD) interface, integrated directly into the astronaut's visor. This makes it possible to quickly identify all key information for nav, comms, dangers and react accordingly.
details:
What ELISAPP does and how it works

Elisapp is installed directly into the helmet and wrist display running on Linux and powered by a Snapdragon chip similar to Ingenuity.

  1. As the astronaut prepares the mission from the Martian base by entering the coordinates of the destination, Elisapp downloads the latest meteorological and topographical data for the route from NASA's database.
  2. Elisapp then calculates the most efficient route in 200 to 400 milliseconds for a 35 km journey, taking into account the start and end points, terrain difficulty, elevation, hazardous areas to avoid, temperature, radiation levels, available oxygen supply, a time limit for the trip and missions based on the points of interest they will encounter. Its built-in trajectory algorithm maintains a 50 m minimum safety corridor preventing proximity to hazardous areas and can calculate a route of up to 500 km in less than a second.
  3. The astronaut can view the map with the planned route and different layers depending on the information he wants to check. When ready, he confirms the mission before departure.
  4. Three satellites in areostationary orbits triangulate the astronaut's position. Meanwhile, their orientation is determined using a system consisting of two antennas mounted on the astronaut's helmet and two phase-shifted signals. With this, the Elisapp user could navigate safely on Mars and access all their information via the heads-up display.

With this, Elisapp could be installed in a rover to enable it to navigate autonomously over very long distances and modify its own route based on fresh meteorological data.
